name: Bilal Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I actually looked up the Panel before I came, read a couple of your reports with an AI summariser on the bus. So I know you're legit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt with a dozer at the Ironbark iron ore mine. Mostly I clean up around the shovels, build the safety bunds along the haul roads, which are the big dirt walls that stop trucks going over the edge, and rip the hard ground so the diggers can get in. I'm not great yet; my bunds come out wavy and the supervisor, Anika, makes me redo them. I love the GPS screen in the cab that shows the design in green and your blade in red. What wears me out is the dust, and twelve hours with my own thoughts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, I was wrong about how fast it'd go. I use AI every day, for study and for my budget, and I'd still say it's useful, just not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be a bit disappointed. I've been getting ready for a big change, and part of me wants it to show up so the getting ready wasn't for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the dozer and finish my Certificate III in surface extraction, which is the proper qualification for my job. I'd keep using the AI tools to study, and keep my name on the list for the remote operations centre in the city in case a seat opens up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Like turning up to a party that got cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. Isn't stability good for someone two years into a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is, and my mum would say I'm mad. But I've watched the GPS on the dozer go from a gimmick to something I can't work without in two years. I'd rather be early than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for in your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I paste in my bank statement and ask where the money went. Turns out I was spending ninety a week on energy drinks. I'm down to about thirty now, and that went into savings.

S0.say: I'd say I was wrong about how fast it would go. I use AI every day for study and budgeting, and I'd still say it's useful, just not magic.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, because I've been getting ready for a big change. Part of me wants it to show up so the preparation wasn't wasted.
S0.do: Keeps running the dozer and finishes his Certificate III in surface extraction using AI tools to study. Keeps his name on the list for the remote operations centre in the city.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a cancelled party.
S0.quote: I've been getting ready for a big change, and part of me wants it to show up so the getting ready wasn't for nothing.
S0.fieldNote: He is the rare junior who would be let down by stability. His readiness for change comes from watching the GPS system on his dozer go from gimmick to essential. The energy drink story shows how casually AI already sits in his daily life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the union to bargain over who gets the gains. If a dozer runs itself, the mine saves a wage, and some of that should go to the workers who trained it, through retraining money or shorter shifts. I'd post that, and I'd get told I'm dreaming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I think I'd be fine, maybe better off. I'm young, I'm into the tech, and I'd be one of the first to move to the remote centre. The people I worry about are the forty-five-year-olds on the crew who've never touched a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chase the remote operations job hard, ring the recruiter every month. I'd do a short course on autonomous mining systems, there's one online at the technical college. And I'd volunteer to be the guy on site who helps the old hands with the new screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe even a bit excited, and guilty about being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my gain is someone else's loss. Danny on my crew has three kids and still prints his roster on paper. If I get the remote seat, it's partly because he didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving to the city for the remote centre bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'm single, I rent, and my flatmate Tomasz is a diesel fitter who'd find work anywhere. The only thing I'd miss is the stars at night shift.

S1.say: I'd say this is the moment for the union to bargain over who gets the gains, through retraining money or shorter shifts. I'd post that and get told I'm dreaming.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd be fine, maybe better off, because I'm young and into the tech. I worry about the older workers on my crew who've never used a tablet.
S1.do: Chases the remote operations centre job, calling the recruiter monthly, and does an online course on autonomous mining systems. Volunteers to help older crew members with the new screens.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with guilt about the excitement.
S1.quote: Danny on my crew has three kids and still prints his roster on paper.
S1.fieldNote: His politics and his self-interest pull in different directions, and he named that himself through guilt about Danny. He would happily move to the city for the remote centre. He sees himself as a bridge for older workers, not just a winner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains from this need to be shared, full stop. A tax on automated mining, paid back to the towns and the workers. I'd be loud about it, because if it isn't sorted in these two years, it never will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my plan breaks. The remote centre was my lifeboat, and in this picture the AI runs the remote centre too. I'd be good at the tech, but if the tech doesn't need anyone, being good at it doesn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the car loan I was about to sign and bank everything. I'd still grab any job going near the automation, even a year of it, because a year of good pay is a cushion. And I'd get properly involved in the campaign for a share of the profits, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it's the first picture where I don't have an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a year of good pay is a cushion. A cushion for what, if there's no work after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question, I don't know. I guess for whatever comes next, a payment from the government or a new kind of job no one's thought of. I'm betting on the world working out a deal, which is a weird bet for someone who reads the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the machines. The people who own them and the politicians who let them keep all of it. The tech is the same either way. Who gets the profit is a choice.

S2.say: I'd say the gains need to be shared, through a tax on automated mining paid back to towns and workers. If it isn't sorted in these two years it never will be.
S2.think: Privately his plan breaks, because AI would run the remote centre that was his lifeboat. Being good at the tech doesn't matter if the tech doesn't need anyone.
S2.do: Drops a planned car loan and saves everything. Takes any job near the automation for even a year of good pay, and gets actively involved in the campaign for a profit share.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicking, and for the first time without an answer.
S2.quote: I'm betting on the world working out a deal, which is a weird bet for someone who reads the news.
S2.fieldNote: His confidence rested on being early to the tech, and he saw quickly that this picture removes that advantage. He is betting on a political deal and laughed at himself for it. Blame goes clearly to owners and politicians, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, more time to make it happen. I'd say the next five years decide whether this is good or terrible, and that depends on policy, not on the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes my plan a lot. I'd get maybe three good years at the remote centre and use them. I think I'd come out with savings and skills, even if the skills have a shelf life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd finish the certificate and take the remote centre job if it came up, even if I had to move. I'd save hard, half my pay if I can, and look at a two-year diploma in something like mechatronics, which is the mix of mechanical and electronic engineering behind robots. And I'd be in the union campaign properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's tight, but tight in a way I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Half your pay is a lot. What would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, the trip to see my cousins, eating out after shift. I'd live like a first-year apprentice on a dozer driver's pay and bank the difference. I did it for six months once, so I know I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the two-year picture you said being good at the tech wouldn't matter. Why does it matter here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three years is time to turn it into money and a qualification. In two years I'd just be learning the screens when the screens disappear. Here I get to cash it in first.

S3.say: I'd say the next five years decide whether this is good or terrible, and that depends on policy, not on the robots. Same message, more time to make it happen.
S3.think: Privately five years gives me about three good years at the remote centre. I'd come out with savings and skills, even if the skills have a shelf life.
S3.do: Finishes his certificate and moves for a remote centre job if one opens. Saves up to half his pay, looks at a two-year mechatronics diploma and joins the union campaign properly.
S3.feel: Uneasy but able to plan around it.
S3.quote: I'd live like a first-year apprentice on a dozer driver's pay and bank the difference.
S3.fieldNote: He explained precisely why five years beats two for him: time to turn early skills into money and a qualification before they expire. The half-pay saving plan is ambitious but he has done it before. His politics stay steady across timelines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right. Pay people to retrain, share the profits, and give towns like ours something to do next. I'd probably say it's a good thing if we get the politics right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well. Ten years is a whole career at my age. I'd ride the automation wave in mining, then move into something AI can't take, or that people still want a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finish the certificate and start the mechatronics diploma part-time. I'd take the remote centre job when it opens and put some savings into a broad index fund each month, because if the robots end up owning everything, I want a small slice of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited even, which I know sounds strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A slice of the robots. Doesn't that sit oddly with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd rather the slice was shared by everyone through a public fund. But until that exists, I'm not going to sit out on principle while my rent goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think people will still want a person for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching, maybe, or looking after people. Tomasz says I'd be a good trainer because I like explaining things. Ten years is enough time to find out if he's right.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it right, with paid retraining, shared profits and something new for towns like ours. It's a good thing if we get the politics right.
S4.think: Privately he expects to do well, because ten years is a whole career at his age. He'd ride automation in mining, then move to work people still want a person for.
S4.do: Finishes his certificate and starts a part-time mechatronics diploma in the first year. Takes the remote centre job when it opens and puts savings monthly into a broad index fund.
S4.quote: if the robots end up owning everything, I want a small slice of the robots.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns the picture almost into an opportunity for him. He admitted the index fund sits oddly with his politics and gave a straight answer about why he'd do it anyway. Teaching or training came up as a possible later path.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me so much, but for Danny and the older guys, and for the town. What would help is a deal that shares the profits from automation, paid out as retraining money and income while people work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people what they'd be glad to stop doing. I wouldn't miss the dust, but I'd miss the crew, and nobody's automating the crew.

headlineQuote: I wouldn't miss the dust, but I'd miss the crew, and nobody's automating the crew.
portrait: Bilal Varga is 27 and drives a dozer at the Ironbark iron ore mine, still redoing wavy safety bunds for his supervisor. He is single, rents with a flatmate, and has a few months saved after using AI to cut his spending. He uses AI every day, is studying for his certificate and has his name down for the remote operations centre. He stays calm in the plateau and steady pictures, gets anxious when AGI in two years wipes out his remote-centre plan, and grows calmer with five and ten years, while consistently arguing that the gains from automation should be shared.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, less for himself than for older crew members like Danny and for the town.
whatWouldHelp: A deal that shares the profits from automation, paid out as retraining money and income while people work out what's next.
